name: Zoe Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Zoe, 27, and I manage a team of twelve customer service agents at a big phone and broadband company's call centre. It's the largest employer on our retail park, a huge grey shed between a carpet shop and a gym. I live with my boyfriend Theo, who drives the number 14 bus, and we rent a small terraced house with a damp back bedroom.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you actually do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My day is half spreadsheets and half people. I start with the call volumes, I listen back to a few calls for quality, and I coach anyone whose numbers have dipped. The best bit is when a new starter handles an angry customer well for the first time and comes off the call grinning. The worst bit is Monday mornings after a network outage, when the queue is three hundred deep and everyone's shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. We tried the AI chatbot on the website last year and customers hated it, half of them asked for a human in the first line. At work I'd say it just confirms what we already knew: people want people when their internet's down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be watching my back. The company has already moved some of the billing calls to a centre abroad, and that had nothing to do with AI. My pay's on the low side for managers here and Theo and I have about three weeks of money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, honestly. I'd keep using the call summary tool, because it saves my agents a couple of minutes per call on notes. And I'd keep nudging my manager about the team leader pay review that keeps getting pushed back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a little restless. The job's not going anywhere in that picture, but it's not going anywhere for me either. I'd still be checking the same queue numbers in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use the summary tool. What does it actually do for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After each call, it writes a short note of what the customer wanted and what we did. Before, my agents typed that themselves and it took ages. It's good, but it gets names wrong, so someone still has to read it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would worry you most if something did go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent, easily, it's more than half of what I take home. Theo's shifts change every month, so his pay goes up and down. If my job wobbled, my boyfriend Theo and I would be behind on rent in about three weeks.

say: Customers **want people** when their internet's down, and the chatbot proved it.
This picture just **confirms** what we already saw at work.
think: The company already **moved calls abroad**, so my job isn't safe anyway.
With **three weeks** of money, any wobble would hurt fast.
do: Keep using the **call summary tool** to save agents time on notes.
Keep pushing my manager about the delayed **pay review**.
Carry on running the team **as normal**.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with a restless sense of being stuck in place.
S0.quote: If my job wobbled, my boyfriend Theo and I would be behind on rent in about three weeks.
fieldNote: She already uses **one AI tool** and judges it fairly, neither fan nor critic.
Her real pressure is **offshoring** and rent, which exist without AI.
She sounds more **restless** than scared in this picture.

steps.text: Keep running the call centre team as normal
Keep using the call summary tool for agents' notes
Push her manager to hold the delayed pay review

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: a phone company that can't speak to its customers isn't a phone company. At work I'd argue for using AI for the notes and the simple stuff, but keeping humans for anything messy. I'd sign every petition going about protecting call centre jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, answering customers is right there on the card, it's literally my team's job. If the simple calls go to a bot, twelve agents becomes six, and they don't need a manager for six. I'd be the one running the redundancy meetings and then probably in one myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the company's AI training properly, not just tick the box, so I'm the manager who knows how to run the bots. I'd join the union, which I've put off because only a few of us are members. And I'd start looking at jobs at the council and the hospital, where people still need to talk to people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad, mainly, and a bit sick. Some of my agents are single mums who chose this job because the shifts fit school. I'd feel like I was helping the company get rid of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn to run the bots. Isn't that helping the company cut jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I hate that. But if someone's going to run the bots, I'd rather it was someone who cares about the people being replaced. It's not a great answer, I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you think of first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kayleigh, who's 22 and has a little boy, and she's my best agent on angry callers. She'd be fine anywhere with people skills, but there's nowhere near us that's hiring. I'd write her the best reference of her life.

say: A phone company that **can't talk to customers** isn't a phone company.
Use AI for **notes and simple calls**, and keep humans for messy problems.
think: **Answering customers** is my team's whole job, so the team halves.
A team of six **doesn't need me**, so I'd likely be cut too.
do: Take the **AI training** seriously so I'm the one who runs the bots.
Apply for **council and hospital** jobs that involve talking to people.
feel: **Sad** and a bit **sick**, especially about agents who are single mums.
S1.quote: If the simple calls go to a bot, twelve agents becomes six, and they don't need a manager for six.
fieldNote: She knows her team's work is **named on the card** and doesn't pretend otherwise.
She admits a **contradiction**: learning the bots that replace her team.
Her biggest concern is **staff with children**, not her own career.

steps.text: Complete the company's AI training properly within three months
Join the union at the call centre
Apply for patient-facing jobs at the council and the hospital

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency rules, now, like in a pandemic. Nobody should lose their income overnight because a company found something cheaper. I'd be posting about it, going to marches, the lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is gone within months of it arriving. All of my work is thinking work, the planning, the coaching, the quality checks. Theo's driving is hands-on, so the bus probably lasts until the robots, around 2031, which would make him the only wage in the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away, I'd stop all spending that isn't rent, food and bills, and put every spare bit aside. I'd look at hands-on care work, because that's people and it's physical, and I'd have three years. Once it arrives, I'd lean on whatever government support exists, and we might move back near my parents, where rent is cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Not frozen, I'd do things, but scared. Two years is nothing when you've only got three weeks of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the robots coming three years later mean for you and Theo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives Theo a few years and not me. It feels odd, because everyone always said my boyfriend's bus job would go first with self-driving buses. In this picture, the people at desks go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you move, if you moved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents live in a smaller town about two hours away. Rent's about a third less and my mum could get me shifts at the care home she works in. It would mean Theo finding a new bus route, which isn't easy either.

say: We need **emergency rules**, like in a pandemic, so incomes don't vanish overnight.
I'd be **marching and posting** about it.
think: My work is **all thinking work**, so the job goes within months.
Theo's **bus driving** lasts until robots, making him the only wage.
do: Cut all spending except **rent, food and bills**.
Train toward **care work**, which is hands-on and people-facing.
Consider **moving near my parents** where rent is a third cheaper.
feel: **Scared but not frozen**, because two years is short with three weeks saved.
S2.quote: Everyone always said my boyfriend's bus job would go first with self-driving buses. In this picture, the people at desks go first.
fieldNote: She notices the **reversal**: her desk job goes before Theo's driving.
She has a **plan**, care work and moving home, but no money to cushion it.
She looks to **government** to step in like an emergency.

steps.text: Cut spending down to rent, food and bills only
Train for care work shifts at her mum's care home
Join marches calling for emergency income rules
Move to her parents' town where rent is a third lower

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do this decently, if the company wants to. I'd push for a proper plan at work: retraining budgets, early warning, help moving people into other roles. I'd say it in the team meetings and on the company forum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd stay as long as I could, because the pay is steady even if it's low. But I'd assume my role is gone by 2031. The question is just whether I'm ready by then or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time course in health and social care at the college, one evening a week. I'd try to save a hundred a month, even if it means no holidays for a few years. And I'd ask Theo to look at getting his coach licence, so he's got more options when the buses change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but in a way I can work with. Five years is enough time to get somewhere, just not much time to make mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said save a hundred a month. Is that realistic for you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if we stop going out at weekends and stop the takeaways, so, just about. We'd probably slip a few months. But even two thousand by 2031 is more than we have ever had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your agents in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my agents the truth: start learning something now, while you've still got a wage. I'd give them time off the phones for courses if the company let me. Some of them would listen and some wouldn't.

say: Five years is **enough time** to do this decently if the company wants to.
Firms need **retraining budgets** and early warning for staff.
think: I'd assume my **role is gone** by 2031, whatever the company promises.
Staying for the **steady wage** makes sense until then.
The real question is whether I'm **ready by 2031**.
do: Start a **health and social care** course one evening a week.
Save **a hundred a month** by cutting weekends out and takeaways.
Ask Theo to get a **coach licence** for more options.
feel: **Worried but workable**, with little room for mistakes.
S3.quote: I'd tell my agents the truth: start learning something now, while you've still got a wage.
fieldNote: With five years she moves from fear to **planning**.
Her savings target is **modest** and she admits it may slip.
She thinks about **Theo's options** as part of the same household plan.

steps.text: Start a health and social care evening course at the college
Save a hundred a month by dropping weekend outings
Help Theo apply for a coach driving licence

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to get this right, so there are no excuses. I'd want unions and the government talking now about what call centre workers do next. I'd probably sound like a broken record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still the same ending for my job. But at 37 I'd hopefully have moved into something people-based already. Ten years takes away the panic, not the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the call centre for a few years while studying part-time for a social work degree, maybe through the Open University. I'd want to be out by about 2033. And we'd probably wait on kids until we know where we're living and working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, almost hopeful. Ten years is a long time, I'd be a different person by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait on kids. Is that a change from your plans now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. We'd talked about thirty or so. With ten years of warning, I'd rather have one stable job between us before a baby comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would get in the way of the social work degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money and tiredness, mostly. It's about six years part-time, and fees aren't cheap. If the company or the government helped with fees, I'd do it, otherwise I might stall halfway.

say: Ten years means there are **no excuses** for getting this wrong.
Unions and government should plan what **call centre workers** do next.
think: The **ending is the same**, just with time to move first.
Ten years removes **the panic**, not the change.
do: Study **social work** part-time while staying at the call centre.
Aim to leave the call centre **by 2033**.
Delay having **children** until jobs and housing are steady.
feel: **Calmer**, almost hopeful, because ten years feels long.
S4.quote: Ten years takes away the panic, not the change.
fieldNote: She treats the decade as a chance for a **full career switch**.
**Fees** are the real obstacle, and she'd stall without help.
She'd **delay children** until work is settled, a quiet but real cost.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time social work degree next year
Leave the call centre for social work by 2033
Wait to have a baby until one job is stable

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My job's all desk work, and with three weeks of savings, two years is no time at all. What would help is help with course fees and some kind of income guarantee while people like me switch to care or social work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask what happens to towns like ours, where the call centre is the main office job. If the call centre closes, there's nothing else on the retail park but a carpet shop and a gym.

headlineQuote: If the call centre closes, there's nothing else on the retail park but a carpet shop and a gym.
portrait: Zoe is 27 and manages **twelve call centre agents** for a big phone and broadband company.
She rents with her boyfriend Theo, a **bus driver**, and they have about three weeks of savings.
She uses one **AI summary tool** and judges new tech once it's proven.
She knows **answering customers** is named on the card and expects her team to halve.
Her plan is a slow move into **care or social work**, held back by fees.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her desk job goes first and savings are tiny.
whatWouldHelp: Help with **course fees** for a move into care or social work.
An **income guarantee** while workers switch careers.
